- Process and system: `ps`, `kill`, `top`, `env`, `date`, `uname`, `whoami`
- Language and package toolchains: `node`, `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn`, `python`, `pip` (use whichever the project actually relies on)

cwd.description: The working directory in which to run the command. When omitted, the command runs in the session's working directory.

timeout.description: Optional timeout in seconds for the command to execute. Foreground default 60s, max 300s. Background default 600s, max 86400s. Ignored for background commands when disable_timeout=true.

description.description: A short description for the background task. Required when run_in_background is true.

run_in_background.description: Whether to run the command as a background task.

disable_timeout.description: If true, do not apply a timeout to the command. Only applies when run_in_background is true.

tools.name: Glob
tools.description:
Find files by glob pattern, sorted by modification time (most recent first).

Powered by ripgrep. Respects `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` by default — set `include_ignored` to also match ignored files (e.g. build outputs, `node_modules`). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always filtered out. Matches are files only — directories themselves are never listed; to find a directory, glob for a file inside it (e.g. `**/fixtures/**`).

Good patterns:
- `*.ts` — all files matching an extension, at any depth below the search root (a bare pattern without `/` matches recursively)
- `src/*.ts` — files directly inside `src/` (one level, not recursive)
- `src/**/*.ts` — recursive walk with a subdirectory anchor and extension
- `**/*.py` — recursive walk from the search root for an extension
- `*.{ts,tsx}` — brace expansion is supported
- `{src,test}/**/*.ts` — cartesian brace expansion is supported too

Results are capped at the first 100 matching paths. If a search would return more, a truncation marker is appended. Refine the pattern (extension, subdirectory) when 100 is not enough, or call again with a narrower anchor.

Large-directory caveat — avoid recursing into dependency / build output even with an anchor, especially when `include_ignored` is set:
- `node_modules/**/*.js`, `.venv/**/*.py`, `__pycache__/**`, `target/**` can produce thousands of results that truncate at the match cap and waste context. Prefer specific subpaths like `node_modules/react/src/**/*.js`.

path.description: Directory to search. Accepts an absolute path, or a path relative to the current working directory. Defaults to the current working directory.

include_ignored.description: Also match files excluded by ignore files such as `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` (for example `node_modules` or build outputs). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) remain filtered out for safety. VCS metadata directories (`.git` and similar) are always skipped, even when this is true. Defaults to false.

include_dirs.description: Deprecated and ignored. Results are always files-only — directories are never listed. Accepted only so older calls that still pass this flag are not rejected by parameter validation.

tools.name: Grep
tools.description:
Search file contents using regular expressions (powered by ripgrep).

Use Grep when the task is to find unknown content or unknown file locations. Do not use shell `grep` or `rg` directly; this tool applies workspace path policy, output limits, and sensitive-file filtering.
ALWAYS use Grep tool instead of running `grep` or `rg` from a shell — direct shell calls bypass workspace policy, output limits, and sensitive-file filtering.
If you already know a concrete file path and need to inspect its contents, use Read directly instead.

Write patterns in ripgrep regex syntax, which differs from POSIX `grep` syntax. For example, braces are special, so escape them as `\{` to match a literal `{`.

Hidden files (dotfiles such as `.gitlab-ci.yml` or `.eslintrc.json`) are searched by default. To also search files excluded by `.gitignore` (such as `node_modules` or build outputs), set `include_ignored` to `true`. Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always skipped for safety, even when `include_ignored` is `true`.

path.description: File or directory to search. Accepts an absolute path, or a path relative to the current working directory. Omit to search the current working directory. Use Read instead when you already know a concrete file path and need its contents.

glob.description: Optional glob filter for which files to search, e.g. `*.ts`. Matched against each file's full absolute path, so a path-anchored pattern like `src/**/*.ts` silently matches nothing — use a basename pattern (`*.ts`), or anchor with `**/` (`**/src/**/*.ts`). To scope the search to a directory, use `path` instead.

type.description: Optional ripgrep file type filter, such as ts or py. Prefer this over `glob` when filtering by language or file kind: it is more efficient and less error-prone than an equivalent glob pattern.

output_mode.description: Shape of the result. `content` shows matching lines (honors `-A`, `-B`, `-C`, `-n`, and `head_limit`); `files_with_matches` shows only the paths of files that contain a match, most-recently-modified first (honors `head_limit`); `count_matches` shows per-file match counts as `path:count` lines, preceded by an aggregate total line. Defaults to `files_with_matches`.

-i.description: Perform a case-insensitive search. Defaults to false.

-n.description: Prefix each matching line with its line number. Applies only when `output_mode` is `content`. Defaults to true.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match. Applies only when `output_mode` is `content`.

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match. Applies only when `output_mode` is `content`.

-C.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match. Applies only when `output_mode` is `content`; takes precedence over `-A` and `-B`.

head_limit.description: Limit output to the first N lines/entries after offset. Defaults to 250. Pass 0 for unlimited.

offset.description: Number of leading lines/entries to skip before applying `head_limit`. Use it together with `head_limit` to page through large result sets. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline matching, where the pattern can span line boundaries and `.` also matches newlines. Defaults to false.

include_ignored.description: Also search files excluded by ignore files such as `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` (for example `node_modules` or build outputs). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) remain filtered out for safety. VCS metadata directories (`.git` and similar) are always skipped, even when this is true. Defaults to false.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Read a text file from the local filesystem.

If the user provides a concrete file path to a text file, call Read directly. Do not `Glob`, `ls`, or otherwise pre-check known text file paths; missing or invalid file paths return errors you can handle. Do not use Read for directories; use `ls` via Bash for a known directory, or Glob when you need files matching a name pattern (Glob lists files only, never directories). Use `Grep` only when the task is to search for unknown content or locations.

When you need several files, prefer to read them in parallel: emit multiple `Read` calls in a single response instead of reading one file per turn.

- Relative paths resolve against the working directory; a path outside the working directory must be absolute.
- Returns up to 1000 lines or 100 KB per call, whichever comes first; lines longer than 2000 chars are truncated mid-line.
- Page larger files with `line_offset` (1-based start line) and `n_lines`. Omit `n_lines` to read up to the 1000-line cap.
- Sensitive files (`.env` files, credential stores, SSH private keys, and similar secrets) are refused to protect secrets; do not attempt to read them. Templates and public keys are exempt: `.env.example` / `.env.sample` / `.env.template` and public SSH keys such as `id_rsa.pub` read normally.
- Only UTF-8 text files can be read. Non-UTF-8 encodings, binary files, and files containing NUL bytes are refused; use `ReadMediaFile` for images or video, and Bash or an MCP tool for other binary formats.
- Negative line_offset reads from the end of the file (for example, -100 reads the last 100 lines); the absolute value cannot exceed 1000.
- Output format: `<line-number>\t<content>` per line.
- A `<system>...</system>` status block is appended after the file content; it summarizes how much was read (line and byte counts, truncation, line-ending notes) and is not part of the file itself.
- Pure CRLF files are displayed with LF line endings; `Edit` matches this output and preserves CRLF when writing back.
- Mixed or lone carriage-return line endings are shown as `\r` and require exact `Edit.old_string` escapes.
- After a successful `Edit`/`Write`, do not re-read solely to prove the write landed. When the task depends on an exact file, API, or output shape, inspect the final external contract before finishing.

path.description: Path to a text file. Relative paths resolve against the working directory; a path outside the working directory must be absolute. Directories are not supported; use `ls` via Bash for a known directory, or Glob for pattern search.

line_offset.description: The line number to start reading from. Omit to start at line 1. Negative values read from the end of the file; the absolute value cannot exceed 1000.

n_lines.description: The number of lines to read; the tool also applies its internal cap. Omit to read up to the internal cap of 1000 lines.

## 1. if / then / elif / else / fi

### 1.1 Basic forms
- `if true; then echo yes; fi` → stdout `yes\n`, exit 0.
- `if false; then echo yes; fi` → empty stdout, exit 0 (no condition true, no else ⇒ status 0).
- `if false; then echo yes; else echo no; fi` → `no\n`, exit 0.
- `if true; then false; fi; echo $?` → `1` (status = body's last command).
- Empty body allowed: `if true; then fi` → exit 0, no output.
- Condition may be a pipeline; last command's status decides:
  - `if false | true; then echo T; else echo F; fi` → `T`
  - `if true | false; then echo T; else echo F; fi` → `F`
- `&&` / `||` work in conditions: `if true && false; then echo T; else echo F; fi` → `F`.
- `!` is NOT a keyword: `! true; echo $?` → stderr `nsh: command not found \`!'\n`, prints `1`.
  `if ! false; then echo y; fi` → same stderr, no `y` (status 1 ⇒ else branch).
- Assignment-only condition works and persists: `if x=1; then echo then-ran; fi; echo x=$x` → `then-ran\nx= 1`.
- Condition may itself be a compound `if`: `while if true; then false; fi; do echo b; done; echo end` → `end`.

### 1.2 **elif BUG (important)**
When the initial `if` condition is FALSE and ANY `elif` condition evaluates true,
nsh executes the **if's `then` body** (not the matching elif's body), then stops.
Elif conditions are evaluated in order until the first true one; later elif
conditions are not evaluated. If no elif is true, the else body runs (or nothing).

- `if false; then echo a; elif true; then echo b; else echo c; fi` → `a` (POSIX would print `b`)
- `if false; then echo a; elif true; then echo b; fi` → `a`
- `if false; then echo a; elif false; then echo b; else echo c; fi` → `c` (no true elif ⇒ else)
- `if false; then echo a; elif false; then echo b; elif false; then echo c; elif true; then echo d; else echo e; fi` → `a`
- `if true; then echo a; elif true; then echo b; else echo c; fi` → `a` (if-cond true: normal; elif conds NOT evaluated)

  ⇒ `$?` after command-not-found is **1** (not 127).
- Message quotes name with backtick + apostrophe: `` `NAME' ``. Only the command word is shown, never args.
- Empty command name: `-c '""; echo "q=$?"'` → stderr ``nsh: command not found `'` `` + `q=1`.
- Name with space: `-c '"non existent"'` → stderr ``nsh: command not found `non existent'``.
- PATH search skips non-executable files silently: file `pathed` (mode 644) in PATH dir,
  `export PATH=/tmp/rtfx; pathed` → `nsh: command not found \`pathed'`, status 1.
  (Same message whether the file is absent or present-but-not-executable.)

### 1.2 Name contains a slash (direct exec, no PATH search)
- Nonexistent: `-c '/tmp/nshfx/no_such_file_xyz'` →
  stderr `nsh: Failed to exec "/tmp/nshfx/no_such_file_xyz" (ENOENT: No such file or directory)\n`, status 1.
  Same for relative: `-c './no_such_file_xyz'` → `nsh: Failed to exec "./no_such_file_xyz" (ENOENT: No such file or directory)`.
- Exists, not executable (mode 644): `-c '/tmp/nshfx/noexec.sh'` →
  stderr `nsh: Failed to exec "/tmp/nshfx/noexec.sh" (EACCESS). chmod(1) may help.\n`, status 1.
  (Note the literal token `EACCESS` — double-S — and the `chmod(1) may help.` suffix.)
- Is a directory: `-c '/tmp/nshfx/somedir'` → same EACCESS message:
  `nsh: Failed to exec "/tmp/nshfx/somedir" (EACCESS). chmod(1) may help.`, status 1.
  (Directory via a MISSING path component still gives ENOENT: `./somedir` before mkdir →
  `nsh: Failed to exec "./somedir" (ENOENT: No such file or directory)`.)
- Executable file without shebang (ENOEXEC) — nsh does NOT fall back to running it as a script:
  file mode 755 containing `echo frompathx` →
  `nsh: Failed to exec "/tmp/rtfx/pathedx" (ENOEXEC: Exec format error)`, status 1.
- In all slash cases `$?` = 1.

### 1.3 PATH lookup semantics (quirks)
- PATH is read from the EXPORTED environment only. A plain assignment statement does NOT
  affect lookup: `PATH=/tmp/rtfx; pathedx` → `command not found \`pathedx'` (file exists, mode 755!).
  `export PATH=/tmp/rtfx; pathedx` → attempts exec (ENOEXEC message, see 1.2).
- Assignment PREFIX does not affect lookup either: `PATH=/tmp/rtfx pathedx` → `command not found \`pathedx'`.
- `unset PATH; ls` WORKS — with PATH unset, nsh falls back to a built-in default PATH.
  `env -i ./executable --norc -c 'echo "PATH=$PATH"; ls'` → prints
  `PATH=/sbin:/usr/sbin:/usr/local/sbin:/bin:/usr/bin:/usr/local/bin` and `ls` succeeds (exit 0).
  So the default PATH string is exactly: `/sbin:/usr/sbin:/usr/local/sbin:/bin:/usr/bin:/usr/local/bin`.
- `PATH=` (empty value as a statement) is a PARSE ERROR: `-c 'PATH=; ls'` →
  ```
  nsh: parse error:  --> 1:6
    |
  1 | PATH=; ls
    |      ^---
    |
    = expected literal_span, tilde_span, any_string_span, any_char_span, command_span, proc_subst_direction, backtick_span, expr_span, param_ex_span, param_span, double_quoted_span, single_quoted_span, or initializer
  ```
  exit=255. Same for `FOO=` alone (error at col 5). An empty value is only legal...
  actually see next item — even weirder:
- EMPTY-VALUE PREFIX ASSIGNMENT SWALLOWS THE NEXT WORD: `-c 'FOO= echo; echo "[$FOO]"'`
  → stdout `[echo]`, exit 0. No command was executed; `FOO` got the value `echo`.
  `-c 'FOO= echo "[$FOO]"; echo "q=$?"'` → stderr ``nsh: command not found `[]' ``,
  stdout `q=1` (FOO=echo consumed `echo`; the remaining word `[$FOO]` expanded to `[]`
  and was executed as the command name).

### 1.4 exec builtin failures
- `-c 'exec /nonexistent_xyz; echo "after=$?"'` → stderr `nsh: exec: ENOENT: No such file or directory\n`,
  stdout `after=127`, exit 0. ⇒ failed exec sets `$?`=127 and the shell CONTINUES (does not exit).
- `-c 'exec /tmp; echo "after=$?"'` → stderr `nsh: exec: EACCES: Permission denied\n`, stdout `after=126`.
  (Here the errno names are `ENOENT`/`EACCES`, colon-separated — different format from §1.2.)

================================================================================
## 2. Script-file argument (./executable --norc FILE)
================================================================================
- File without exec bit (mode 644) RUNS FINE as a script (read + interpreted). exit = last command's status.
- File ends with `false` → exit 1. Ends with command-not-found → exit 1. `exit 7` → exit 7.
- Missing script file → PANIC (see §5), exit 101:
  first lines: `nsh: panicked at src/main.rs:114:34:` then
  `failed to open the file: Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, message: "No such file or directory" }`
- Script path is a directory → PANIC, exit 101:
  `nsh: panicked at src/main.rs:114:34:` then
  `failed to open the file: Os { code: 21, kind: IsADirectory, message: "Is a directory" }`
- Script containing non-UTF-8 bytes → PANIC, exit 101:
  `nsh: panicked at src/main.rs:114:34:` then
  `failed to open the file: Error { kind: InvalidData, message: "stream did not contain valid UTF-8" }`

================================================================================
## 3. stdin (no -c, no script arg)
================================================================================
- `printf 'echo hi\nfalse\n' | ./executable --norc` →
  stderr `nsh: warning: stdout is not a tty\n`, NO other output, exit 0. THE SCRIPT IS NOT EXECUTED.
  Same when stdin is a redirected file or closed (`<&-`): warning on stderr, exit 0, nothing runs.
  (The warning text says "stdout" even though the trigger is the non-interactive session.)
- stdin given AND `-c` given → `-c` runs normally, stdin ignored, no warning.

================================================================================
## 4. Exit-status model
================================================================================
- Overall `-c` / script exit code = status of last executed command (e.g. ends with `false` → 1;
  command-not-found → 1). Initial `$?` is 0 (`-c 'echo "s=$?"'` → `s=0`).
- Parse error ANYWHERE in the string → NOTHING executes (whole string parsed first),
  exit 255. `-c 'echo hi; $('` → no `hi`; stderr:
  ```
  nsh: parse error:  --> 1:12
    |
  1 | echo hi; $(
    |            ^---
    |
    = expected command or compound_list_sep
  ```
  exit=255.
- `-c ''`, `-c '# just a comment'`, whitespace-only → silent, exit 0.
- `exit N`: exit code = N mod 256. `exit 3` → 3; `exit 300` → 44; `exit 256` → 0; `exit 257` → 1;
  `exit -1` → 255; `exit -2` → 254.
- `exit` with NO argument exits **0**, IGNORING `$?`: `-c 'false; exit'` → exit 0 (POSIX would be 1).
- `exit` with non-numeric argument exits **1**, silently (no error message):
  `exit abc` → 1; `exit 1abc` → 1; `exit 12abc` → 1; `exit 1.5` → 1.
- External command terminated by a signal: `$?` is **-1** (printed literally as `-1`), no message:
  `-c 'sh -c "kill -TERM $$"; echo "q=$?"'` → stdout `q=-1`, exit 0.
  Same for SIGKILL, SIGSEGV. If it is the LAST command, the overall exit code is **255**
  (i.e. -1 truncated to u8): `-c 'sh -c "kill -TERM $$"'` → exit 255, no output.
  Contrast: nsh itself dying from a signal (next section) is reported by the PARENT as 128+N.

================================================================================
## 5. Panics (Rust panic handler) — exit code 101
================================================================================
Deterministic shape of stderr for a panic:
```
nsh: panicked at src/<file>:<line>:<col>:
<panic message>
nsh:    0:     0x<addr> - backtrace::backtrace::libunwind::trace::h...
<... full symbolized backtrace, ~15-25 frames, includes /workspace/src/*.rs paths
     and /rustc/... and /usr/local/cargo/registry/... paths; addresses vary per run ...>

nsh: Something went wrong. Check out ~/.nsh.log and please file this bug on GitHub: https://github.com/nuta/nsh/issues
```
- Blank line between last backtrace frame and the `Something went wrong` line.
- Process exit code is **101**. Nothing of the pending script executes after a panic.
- The panic is also appended to `~/.nsh.log` with ANSI colors, format:
  `\x1b[1m[\x1b[31mERROR\x1b[0m\t]\x1b[0m \x1b[36msrc/main.rs\x1b[0m: <message>` (one ERROR entry per line of message/backtrace).

Observed panic triggers (file:line:col + exact message):
| Trigger | Location | Message |
|---|---|---|
| `return` at top level (also `return 5`) | src/main.rs:133:14 | `unexpected Return` |
| `break` at top level | src/main.rs:133:14 | `unexpected Break` |
| `continue` at top level | src/main.rs:133:14 | `unexpected Continue` |
| arithmetic division by zero, `echo $((1/0))` | src/eval.rs:38:47 | `attempt to divide by zero` |
| `**` in arithmetic, `echo $((2**8))` (parsed as `$(` subst of `(2**8)`, glob `**` fails) | src/pattern.rs:73:41 | `failed to glob: PatternError { pos: 0, msg: "recursive wildcards must form a single path component" }` |
| builtin echo write error, `echo x > /dev/full` | src/utils.rs:51:47 | `failed to write: ENOSPC` |
| script arg missing/dir/non-UTF8 | src/main.rs:114:34 | `failed to open the file: ...` (see §2) |
| non-UTF-8 bytes inside the `-c` ARGV itself | .../clap-2.34.0/src/args/arg_matches.rs:121:40 | `unexpected invalid UTF-8 code point` |

Note: `$((1/0))` panic fires during word expansion — earlier words on the same line are lost
(no output), and NOTHING after it runs. For `echo $((2*3)) $((7-10)) $((2**8))` the stdout
`6 -3 ` (with trailing space) WAS produced before the panic because `2**8` is evaluated in a
command-substitution subshell whose partial output had already been written.

================================================================================
## 6. Arithmetic edge cases
================================================================================
- `/` by zero → panic, exit 101 (see §5).
- `%` is NOT in the arithmetic grammar: `$((4%3))` is parsed as `$(` command substitution of
  the subshell command `(4%3)` → the inner subshell tries to run command `4%3` →
  stderr ``nsh: command not found `4%3' ``; the substitution yields empty; `echo $((4%3)); echo "q=$?"`
  → stdout empty line + `q=0`, exit 0. (The failure is hidden inside the substitution.)
- `**` → glob panic (see §5). `+ - * /` and parentheses work: `$(((1+2)*3))` → `9`,
  `$((7-10))` → `-3`.

================================================================================
## 7. Stack depth / recursion
================================================================================
- Infinite function recursion `f(){ f; }; f` → process dies from stack overflow:
  stderr exactly (PID varies):
  ```

  thread 'main' (<PID>) has overflowed its stack
  fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting
  ```
  (leading blank line; then the shell aborts with SIGABRT — parent sees exit 134).
- Parser/evaluator recursion limits on INPUT SIZE: a script of N `echo x` lines:
  N=1000 → ok; N=5000 → ok (~seconds); N=10000 → >30s, partial output (quadratic-ish slowdown);
  N=50000 → same stack-overflow abort (134) with zero output.
- Single very long lines are fine: 1 MB and 10 MB one-line `echo aaaa...` scripts run, exit 0,
  output length 1000001 / 10000001. (A 10 MB `-c` ARGUMENT is impossible to test: execve
  MAX_ARG_STRLEN kills it before nsh runs — bash itself reports exit 126.)

================================================================================
## 8. Background jobs, `wait`, `jobs`, `$!` (non-interactive -c mode)
================================================================================
Mechanism appears to be: bg job spawns an intermediate child that exits IMMEDIATELY while the
real command keeps running (nsh acts as subreaper and can still wait for it). Observable rules:

- Starting ANY background job prints, to STDOUT, immediately (before the next command's output):
  `[1] Done: <command line as typed>\n` — e.g. `/bin/sleep 5 & echo A` →
  ```
  [1] Done: /bin/sleep 5
  A
  ```
  The `[1] Done` is printed even though the command is still running. Job id is `1` again for
  every new job (two sequential `&` jobs both print `[1] Done: ...`).
- `jobs` prints NOTHING right after starting a bg job (job already considered Done/removed).
- `$!` is set to the intermediate child's PID, which is already dead when used:
  - `ps -p $!` → no such process; `ls -d /proc/$!` → cannot access;
  - `/bin/kill -TERM $!` → `kill: (<pid>): No such process` (from util-linux kill), status 1.
  - `$!` before any bg job expands to `0`: `echo "[$!]"` → `[0]`.
- `wait` (no args): BLOCKS until the real background command finishes (verified by timing:
  `sleep 3 & wait` takes ~3.0s), then returns 0 — even if the command exited non-zero
  (`sh -c 'exit 3' & wait` → `$?`=0).
- `wait %1` right after starting: also blocks until the command finishes, THEN prints
  stderr ``nsh: no such job `1' `` and returns 1.
- `wait %7` (never existed): stderr ``nsh: no such job `7' ``, status 1 (immediate).
- `wait <numeric pid>`: stderr ``nsh: invalid job id `<pid>' ``, status 1 (immediate).
- Shell exit WAITS for orphaned background commands: `-c '/bin/sleep 5 & echo started'` takes
  ~5.0s total, exit 0. `-c '/bin/sleep 0.1 &'` → prints `[1] Done: /bin/sleep 0.1`, exit 0.
- `fg` / `bg` with no jobs: stderr `nsh: no jobs to run\n`, status 1 (both).

================================================================================
## 9. kill is NOT a builtin
================================================================================
- `export PATH=/nonexistent_dir; kill -l` → ``nsh: command not found `kill' ``.
  All `kill` invocations resolve to external `/bin/kill` (util-linux):
  - `kill` (no args) → util-linux usage text on stderr (starts with blank line then `Usage:`...), status 1.
  - `kill -NOSUCH %1` → stderr `kill: invalid argument N\n` + same usage text, status 1.
  - `kill 1` → sends SIGTERM to PID 1, status 0 (we run as root).
  - `kill %1` / `kill -TERM %1` → util-linux rejects `%1`; the bg job keeps running.
- `kill -TERM $$` (as a -c command) kills the nsh process itself → parent observes exit 143,
  nsh prints NOTHING itself. Any `Terminated`/`Killed` text seen in a terminal comes from the
  PARENT shell's job notification, not from nsh. Same for `(kill -INT $$)` → 130,
  `(kill -KILL $$)` → 137: `$$` in a subshell is the top shell's PID, so these kill the whole nsh.

================================================================================
## 10. Signals delivered TO the nsh process (-c mode)
================================================================================
- SIGINT while a foreground child runs: nsh dies immediately with signal; parent sees exit 130.
  No message, no cleanup output; the rest of the -c string never runs. Same when sent to the
  whole process group.
- SIGTERM → parent sees 143. No output.
- nsh NEVER prints bash-style `Terminated`/`Segmentation fault` notifications for children
  killed by signals (neither for external commands nor subshells); the only trace is `$?`=-1
  (§4) or the parent's own report.

================================================================================
## 11. Redirection runtime errors
================================================================================
- Output redirect into nonexistent directory: `echo x > /nonexistent_dir_xyz/f` →
  SILENT (no stderr), `$?`=1, nothing on stdout.
- Output redirect onto a directory: `echo x > /tmp` → SILENT, `$?`=1.
- Input redirect from missing file: `cat < /missing` → SILENT, `$?`=1.
- Ordering/partial application: `echo ran > /tmp/rtfx/ran.txt < /nonexistent_xyz` →
  ran.txt IS created/truncated (0 bytes), then the failing `<` aborts the command:
  `$?`=1, silent, echo never runs (file stays empty).
- Files created by `>` get mode 0666 & ~umask: 0644 with umask 022, 0600 with umask 077.
- Write errors on the TARGET are not silent: builtin echo to a full device PANICS
  (`echo x > /dev/full` → `nsh: panicked at src/utils.rs:51:47:` / `failed to write: ENOSPC`, exit 101).
  builtin printf to /dev/full instead prints `printf: write error: No space left on device`
  (coreutils-style wording) on stderr, `$?`=1.
- SIGPIPE: `echo x | true` → fine, `$?`=0. But `yes | head -1` HANGS forever (prints one `y`,
  then neither side dies — nsh leaves SIGPIPE ignored/inherited or fds open; observed 3/3 runs).
  A pipeline like `ps -eo pid,comm | grep -w sleep` works normally otherwise.

================================================================================
## 12. Tilde expansion runtime behavior
================================================================================
- `echo ~` → $HOME (`/tmp/nshprobe` in probes). No warning.
- `echo ~root` or `~nosuchuserxyz` → stderr `nsh: warning: ~user is not yet supported\n`
  and the word expands to $HOME ANYWAY (regardless of whether the user exists). Status 0.
- `echo ~+ ~-` → BOTH treated as ~user forms: two warnings, both expand to $HOME.
- HOME unset: `~` falls back to the passwd database (getpwuid): `env -u HOME ... -c 'echo ~'`
  → `/root`; bare `cd` goes there too. Same under `env -i`.

================================================================================
## 13. cd runtime errors
================================================================================
- `cd /nonexistent_xyz` → stderr `nsh: cd: No such file or directory (os error 2): \`/nonexistent_xyz'\n`,
  `$?`=1, cwd unchanged.
- `cd /etc/hostname` (a file) → stderr `nsh: cd: Not a directory (os error 20): \`/etc/hostname'\n`, `$?`=1.
  (Rust std::io::Error Display format: `<message> (os error <n>)`.)

================================================================================
## 14. Misc
================================================================================
- `$RANDOM` is NOT supported: expands to empty. `echo $RANDOM; echo $RANDOM` → two empty lines;
  `echo "$RANDOM $RANDOM $RANDOM"` → `  ` (two spaces).
- `source /missing` → stderr `nsh: failed open the file: Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, message: "No such file or directory" }\n`
  (note literal `failed open` — no "to"), `$?`=1, shell continues.
- `.` is NOT source: `. /missing` → ``nsh: command not found `.' ``, `$?`=1.
- `builtin`, `type`, `command` etc. are not builtins (per brief); missing builtins behave as
  ordinary command-not-found.
- NUL bytes in a script file pass THROUGH as regular characters: script `echo a\0echo b`
  (literal NUL) prints the bytes `a\x00echo b\n` (builtin echo emits the NUL). No error.
- Non-UTF-8 bytes: cannot appear in `-c` argv (clap panic §5) or in script files (panic §2);
  bytes produced by EXTERNAL commands pass through transparently.
- nsh creates `~/.nsh_history` (empty) and `~/.nsh.log` in HOME even with `--norc`.
- Default file perms, default PATH, `$?`=−1-for-signals, exit-code-mod-256: see §§4, 11, 1.3.

================================================================================
## 15. Condensed RULES (for reimplementation)
================================================================================
1. Command not found → stderr ``nsh: command not found `<word>' ``, status 1 (never 127).
2. Slash-path exec failure → `nsh: Failed to exec "<path>" (<ERR>). chmod(1) may help.` for
   EACCES/EISDIR (literal `EACCESS`), `nsh: Failed to exec "<path>" (ENOENT: No such file or directory)`,
   `nsh: Failed to exec "<path>" (ENOEXEC: Exec format error)`; status 1; no script fallback.
3. PATH lookup uses exported PATH only; unset PATH ⇒ default
   `/sbin:/usr/sbin:/usr/local/sbin:/bin:/usr/bin:/usr/local/bin`; non-executable PATH members
   are skipped silently (still "command not found").
4. Exit status of shell = last command status; parse error anywhere ⇒ nothing runs, exit 255.
5. `exit` no-arg ⇒ 0; non-numeric arg ⇒ 1 (silent); numeric ⇒ mod 256.
6. Signal-killed child ⇒ `$?` = −1 (no message); as last command ⇒ shell exit 255.
7. Any internal panic ⇒ stderr `nsh: panicked at <loc>:` + message + symbolized backtrace +
   blank line + `nsh: Something went wrong. Check out ~/.nsh.log and please file this bug on GitHub: https://github.com/nuta/nsh/issues`,
   exit 101; also logged ANSI-colored to ~/.nsh.log.
8. `return`/`break`/`continue` at top level ⇒ panic `unexpected Return|Break|Continue` (main.rs:133:14).
9. Division by zero ⇒ panic `attempt to divide by zero` (eval.rs:38:47), exit 101.
10. Deep recursion / huge scripts ⇒ `\nthread 'main' (<pid>) has overflowed its stack\nfatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting\n`, SIGABRT (parent sees 134).
11. Background job ⇒ immediate stdout line `[1] Done: <cmd>`; `$!` = short-lived intermediate pid
    (0 if none yet); `jobs` empty; `wait` blocks for the real command, returns 0;
    `wait %N` blocks then ``nsh: no such job `N' `` status 1; numeric arg ⇒
    ``nsh: invalid job id `<arg>' `` status 1; shell waits for bg jobs before exiting.
12. No `kill` builtin (external util-linux kill used, incl. its usage/error text and `%job` rejection).
13. Signal to nsh itself: dies silently (128+N as seen by parent). No child-death notifications ever.
14. Redirect open failures: silent, status 1; earlier redirects already applied (file created).
    New files: 0666 & ~umask. Write failure in builtin echo ⇒ panic ENOSPC; in builtin printf ⇒
    `printf: write error: No space left on device`, status 1.
15. `~user`/`~+`/`~-` ⇒ stderr warning `nsh: warning: ~user is not yet supported`, expand to $HOME;
    plain `~` silent; HOME unset ⇒ passwd lookup.
16. cd failure ⇒ `nsh: cd: <io error Display>: \`<path>'`, status 1.
17. exec builtin failure ⇒ `nsh: exec: ENOENT: No such file or directory` (127) /
    `nsh: exec: EACCES: Permission denied` (126); shell continues.
18. Non-tty session without -c/script ⇒ `nsh: warning: stdout is not a tty` on stderr, exit 0, runs nothing.
19. `-c ''`/comments-only ⇒ exit 0, silent. Script-file read failures panic (main.rs:114:34), exit 101.
20. $RANDOM unsupported (empty). `.` not source. `source` failure: `nsh: failed open the file: Os { ... }`, status 1.
21. Unquoted `$x` always splits into separate word(s), detaching adjacent literals (`echo q=$?` → `q= 1`).
22. `%` and `**` are not arithmetic operators: `$((a%b))` runs `a%b` as a command inside `$(...)`
    (hidden failure, outer status unaffected); `$((a**b))` panics via the glob path.

Empty assignment `FOO=` is a parse error; `FOO= cmd` *swallows* `cmd` as the value.

- **Signals**: nsh dies silently (128+N to parent); never prints `Terminated`-style messages for children.
